'''Tsiolkovskiy''' is a large [[Lunar craters|lunar]] [[impact crater]] that is located on the [[Far side (Moon)|far side]] of the [[Moon]].  Named for Russian scientist [[Konstantin Tsiolkovsky]],<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.nasa.gov/mission_pages/LRO/multimedia/lroimages/201000430_tsiol.html|title = NASA - Floor of Tsiolkovskiy - Exploration Region of Interest}}</ref> it lies in the southern hemisphere, to the west of the large crater [[Gagarin (crater)|Gagarin]], and northwest of [[Milne (crater)|Milne]]. Just to the south is [[Waterman (crater)|Waterman]], with [[Neujmin (crater)|Neujmin]] to the south-southwest.  The crater protrudes into the neighbouring [[Fermi (crater)|Fermi]], an older crater of comparable size that does not have a [[lava]]-flooded floor.

Tsiolkovskiy has been considered one of the largest craters of the Upper (Late) [[Imbrian]] age,<ref>[https://pubs.er.usgs.gov/publication/pp1348 The geologic history of the Moon].  [[USGS]] Professional Paper 1348. By [[Don Wilhelms|Don E. Wilhelms]], John F. McCauley, and Newell J. Trask.  U.S. Government Printing Office, Washington: 1987.  Table 11.2.</ref><ref>{{cite journal |date=1988 |first=A. |last=Tyrie |title=Age dating of mare in the lunar crater Tsiolkovsky by crater-counting method |pages=245-264 |doi=10.1007/bf00058489 |journal=Earth, Moon, and Planets |issn=0167-9295 |volume=42}}</ref> although that dating was revised to the Imbrian/[[Eratosthenian]] boundary in 2013.<ref>{{cite book |date=2013 |first=J.-P. |last=Williams |display-authors=etal |chapter=Inferred age of Mare Fill in Tsiolkovskiy Crater: Constraints on the preservation of exterior impact melt deposits |chapter-url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/236621067 |title=44th Lunar and Planetary Science Conference}}</ref> A number of sites on its walls and central peak have slopes over 45°, leading some to propose a Late Eratosthenian dating.<ref>{{cite journal |date=2016 |first1=Mikhail A. |last1=Kreslavsky |first2=James W. |last2=Head |title=The  steepest  slopes  on  the  Moon  from  Lunar  Orbiter  Laser  Altimeter (LOLA)  Data:  Spatial  Distribution  and  Correlation  with  Geologic Features |pages=329-336 |doi=10.1016/j.icarus.2016.02.036 |journal=Icarus |eissn=1090-2643 |volume=273|doi-access=free }}</ref>{{rp|333}}

==Characteristics==
Tsiolkovskiy is one of the most prominent features on the far side of the Moon. It possesses high, [[wiktionary:terrace|terrace]]d inner walls and a well-formed central peak, which rises over 3200 m above the floor of the crater. The floor is unusual for a crater on the far side, as it is covered by the dark-hued [[Lunar mare|mare]] that is characteristic of the maria found on the near side. The distribution of the mare material is not symmetrical across the floor, but is instead more heavily concentrated to the east and south. There is also a protruding bay of darker material that reaches the wall to the west-northwest. The remainder of the floor has the same [[albedo]] as the terrain surrounding the crater.

The crater has an unusually high [[rockfall]] density for its diameter, although this does not apply to its northwest rim.<ref>{{cite journal |date=2020-06-08 |first=Valentin Tertius |last=Bickel |display-authors=etal |title=Impacts drive lunar rockfalls over billions of years |pages=1-7 |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/342008792 |doi=10.1038/s41467-020-16653-3 |journal=Nature Communications |eissn=2041-1723 |volume=11|pmc=7280507 }}</ref>{{rp|2}}

A row of small craters in [[Mendeleev (crater)|Mendeleev]] crater far to the northeast is called Catena Mendeleev, and the row points directly at Tsiolkovsky.  For this reason the craters are believed to be [[secondary crater|secondaries]] from the Tsiolkovsky impact.<ref>The geologic history of the Moon, 1987, [[Donald Wilhelms|Wilhelms, Don E.]]; with sections by McCauley, John F.; Trask, Newell J. [[United States Geological Survey|USGS]] Professional Paper: 1348.  Figure 9.26 B ([https://pubs.er.usgs.gov/publication/pp1348 online])</ref>

This feature was discovered on photographs sent back by the Russian spacecraft [[Luna 3]], and was subsequently imaged by several of the American [[Lunar Orbiter program|Lunar Orbiters]] and then by [[Apollo program|Apollo]] astronauts.

[[Apollo 17]] Astronaut [[Harrison Schmitt|Harrison "Jack" Schmitt]] and other scientists (Schmitt was the only trained scientist, a [[geologist]], to walk on the Moon) strongly advocated Tsiolkovskiy as the landing site of  Apollo 17, using small communications satellites deployed from the [[Apollo Command/Service Module|Command/Service Module]] for communication from the far side of the Moon. [[NASA]] vetoed the idea as too risky, and Apollo 17 instead landed in the [[Taurus–Littrow valley]] on December 11, 1972.
